title: Legal Procedures: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam and Court Powers

steps.title: Evolution of substantive criminal law in India
steps.tx: Replacing the Indian Penal Code of 1860, the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita codification** serves as the primary substantive criminal statute defining offences, culpable mental states, and punitive measures across India. Medical practitioners frequently interface with this statute when documenting blunt force trauma, firearm lacerations, sexual offences, unnatural fatalities, dowry harassment, poisoned casualties, and clinical negligence disputes before criminal trial benches.
steps.say: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaces the Indian Penal Code. It defines offences and punishments, guiding doctors who examine trauma, sexual assault, poisoning, and clinical negligence.

rows: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder

steps.title: Grievous hurt criteria under modern statute
steps.tx: In medicolegal injury certification, the statutory **grievous hurt legal criteria** dictate elevated criminal culpability whenever physical violence causes permanent privation of sight, hearing, limb amputation, facial disfigurement, bone fracture, or joint dislocation. Crucially, clause eight classifies any injury that endangers life or causes the victim to remain in severe bodily pain or unable to follow ordinary pursuits for twenty days as grievous.
steps.say: Grievous hurt covers loss of sight, hearing, limbs, permanent facial disfigurement, fractures, tooth loss, life-endangering trauma, or inability to perform daily activities for twenty days.

steps.title: Medical negligence provisions under Section 106 BNS
steps.tx: Under criminal law reform, the **medical practitioner negligence proviso** in Section 106(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita establishes distinct statutory sentencing parameters for registered doctors. While general rash or negligent acts resulting in death carry imprisonment up to five years, clinical negligence by a registered medical practitioner during a professional medical procedure carries a mitigated ceiling of two years imprisonment along with fines.
steps.say: Section 106 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita reduces the maximum prison term for registered doctors to two years for procedural medical negligence, recognizing clinical risk.

steps.title: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam and evidentiary rules
steps.tx: Replacing the Indian Evidence Act of 1872, the **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam enactment** governs all rules of evidence, admissibility, witness competence, and expert testimony in judicial trials. Medical witnesses present documentary evidence comprising injury sheets, postmortem reports, and chemical analysis certificates, which transition from ordinary hearsay into admissible trial records through oral corroboration and cross-examination in open court.
steps.say: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam replaces the Evidence Act. It sets rules for admitting injury certificates, autopsy reports, and expert medical testimony in trials.

steps.title: Expert medical witness testimony under Section 39 BSA
steps.tx: When a court forms an opinion regarding forensic science, toxicology, cause of death, or biological identity, the **expert witness testimony framework** under Section 39 BSA permits medical officers to state expert opinions. Unlike ordinary witnesses who may testify only to observed facts, a medical expert is legally permitted to interpret findings, deduce injury mechanisms, estimate time since death, and reconstruct wound trajectories.
steps.say: Under Section 39 of the evidence statute, medical experts can provide professional opinions on injury mechanisms, weapon types, and time since death, unlike lay witnesses.

left.title: Common witness of fact
points: Testifies only to facts directly perceived
Cannot offer scientific deductions or guesses

right.title: Expert medical witness
points: Can offer scientific opinions and deductions

steps.title: Hierarchy and sentencing powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts
steps.tx: The criminal judiciary in India follows a strict jurisdictional ladder, headed by the **constitutional court sentencing authority** vested in the Supreme Court and state High Courts. The Supreme Court operates as the ultimate appellate authority, while state High Courts possess statutory power to pass any sentence authorized by law, including capital punishment, life imprisonment, and supervisory review over all lower subordinate criminal benches.
steps.say: The Supreme Court and state High Courts hold apex judicial authority. High Courts can pass any lawful sentence, including life imprisonment and capital punishment.

steps.title: Sessions Court and Additional Sessions Judge powers
steps.tx: At the district tier, the presiding **Sessions Court criminal jurisdiction** exercises trial authority over major offences including homicide, dowry murder, rape, and major dacoity. A Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge may pass any sentence authorized by law; however, any sentence of capital death awarded by a Sessions Court remains legally suspended until formally confirmed by a division bench of the respective state High Court.
steps.say: Sessions Judges can award any lawful sentence including life imprisonment, but any death sentence must be confirmed by the High Court before execution.

steps.title: Subordinate magistrate sentencing powers
steps.tx: Governing primary criminal trials, the **subordinate judicial magistrate powers** define the jurisdictional limits of daily courtroom sentencing. A Chief Judicial Magistrate or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate can impose imprisonment up to seven years. A Judicial Magistrate of the First Class (JMFC) can pass imprisonment terms up to three years, whereas a Second Class Magistrate is restricted to imprisonment not exceeding one year.
steps.say: Chief Judicial Magistrates can sentence up to seven years. First Class Magistrates can sentence up to three years, while Second Class Magistrates are capped at one year.

steps.title: Electronic records and digital evidentiary certificates
steps.tx: With the modernization of procedural law, statutory rules enforce **electronic evidence digital certification** under Section 63 BSA for electronic medical records, digital hospital monitors, ECG printouts, CT scan DICOM files, and mortuary videography. The treating clinician or hospital IT custodian must submit a signed compliance certificate verifying device integrity, uninterrupted operation, and authenticity before electronic printouts are admitted into legal evidence.
steps.say: Digital hospital records, CT scans, and mortuary videos require an electronic certificate under Section 63 BSA confirming device security before court admission.
